opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that the current agent paradigm is basically taking a pretrained model, doing a bunch of post-training to make it good at following instructions and using tools, and then putting it in a loop where it can take actions, see the results, and keep going. What we've been watching pretty closely is how long a task these systems can reliably complete. One way to think about that is the length of task, measured in how long it would take a skilled human, that the model can do with some decent probability of success. That number has been going up pretty steadily, roughly doubling every several months, and that's been surprisingly consistent across a bunch of different model generations.

If you take that trend seriously and extrapolate it, you get to a place where agents can do tasks that take a human days or weeks fairly soon. A lot of AI research and development is made of exactly those kinds of tasks: implement this idea, run these experiments, debug why training is unstable, write the infrastructure, analyze the results. It's not that you need some totally new paradigm. You need the existing thing to get more reliable over longer horizons, better at noticing when it's gone wrong and recovering, and better at managing its own context and plan over a long stretch of work.

I don't think it'll happen as one discrete jump. It's more that you first get agents that speed up individual researchers on well-scoped engineering tasks, which is already starting. Then they take on bigger chunks with less supervision. Eventually the humans are mostly setting direction and checking results, and the bottleneck shifts to compute and to how good the models' research taste is. Taste, meaning which experiments are worth running and which results are actually interesting, is the part I'm least sure about. It's harder to measure, and it's plausible it lags behind raw engineering ability.

The reason this matters so much from a safety and evaluation perspective is the feedback loop. If AI systems can substantially accelerate AI research, progress could get a lot faster than our current intuitions suggest, and the window for noticing problems and responding to them shrinks. So a big part of what I think we need is good measurement. We need to track these capabilities carefully, with realistic tasks, and be honest about the uncertainty. Benchmarks can be misleading in both directions. Models can look better than they are because the tasks are too clean, or worse than they are because the scaffolding is bad or we didn't elicit their full capability. Getting that right is, I think, one of the more important things to do in the next couple of years.

r002.rationale: It says, “It's not that you need some totally new paradigm,” and describes extending current agents with greater reliability over longer tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that a lot of what we see today already looks like the early, clunky version of that. If you take the current agent scaffolding — a model in a loop with a shell, a code editor, some way to run experiments and read the results — that's structurally not that different from what a junior researcher does. The difference is mostly in how long they can sustain coherent work before things fall apart.

That's actually the thing we spend a lot of time measuring at METR. We try to characterise agent capability in terms of the length of task, measured in human time, that a model can complete reliably. And the striking thing is how fast that's moving. A couple of years ago you were looking at tasks that take a human a few minutes. Now you're looking at tasks in the hours range, with the trend doubling something like every several months. If that trend continues, you're not that many doublings away from "a week of a skilled engineer's work," and at that point you've crossed a pretty important threshold for R&D automation, because a lot of ML research decomposes into chunks of roughly that size: set up an experiment, debug it, iterate on it, write up what happened.

So the path I'd expect is not some new paradigm. It's the current paradigm with the failure modes sanded down. Right now agents fail in ways that are kind of embarrassing — they lose track of what they were doing, they declare success when tests are still failing, they go around in circles on a bug a human would recognise in thirty seconds. Those are the bottlenecks. As those get fixed, the main constraint shifts from "can the model do the thing" to "can we give it the right environment, the right feedback loops, enough compute to run many experiments in parallel." And labs have very strong incentives to build exactly that, because speeding up your own research is the highest-leverage thing you can do.

The bit that I think people underweight is that research automation is somewhat self-accelerating. Once the agents are good enough to meaningfully contribute to improving the next generation of agents, you get a loop, and the dynamics of that loop are genuinely hard to predict. That's why we care so much about having good measurements before we're in it rather than after. It's also why I'm cautious about anyone saying confidently "this won't happen for a decade" or "this is two years away." The evaluations we have are imperfect, the tasks we use are easier than real research in important ways — there's a clean success criterion, there's no messy institutional context — and real research is bottlenecked on things like taste and knowing which questions are worth asking, which we are much worse at measuring.

So my overall picture is: continuous progress along the current trajectory, with a real chance that it gets us to substantial R&D automation within a handful of years, and a lot of uncertainty about exactly when the hard parts give way. The thing I'd most want is for the people building these systems to be tracking that trajectory carefully enough that nobody is surprised when it does.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how long a task these systems can carry out reliably without a human stepping in. There’s a big difference between answering a question about some code and taking a research objective, figuring out what experiments to run, implementing them, interpreting the results, and deciding what to do next.

The agent setup gives you a way to connect those steps. The model can use tools, execute code, observe what happened, and revise its approach. But having that loop doesn’t automatically make it a good researcher. It needs to notice when an experiment is misleading, when its approach isn’t working, or when it’s quietly changed the question it was supposed to answer. Small mistakes can compound over a long task.

So I’d expect progress to look like humans delegating increasingly large pieces of research. Initially, you might hand over a well-specified experiment. Then you might hand over a question and ask the system to design the experiments. Eventually, it could take responsibility for a whole research direction, with much less supervision.

AI research itself is particularly consequential here, because improvements to the system could make it better at producing further improvements. That doesn’t mean an agent loop immediately gives you runaway progress—experiments, compute, and evaluating ideas can still be bottlenecks. But I think the ability to do useful research autonomously is a much more significant threshold than being able to give impressive answers in a conversation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key transition is from systems that can do a well-specified task to systems that can work out what tasks are worth doing. In research, you don’t just need to write code or run an experiment. You need to choose a question, notice when your approach isn’t working, interpret an ambiguous result, and decide what to try next.

The agent paradigm gives you a way to connect those activities: a model can use tools, observe what happened, and take another action. But having that loop doesn’t automatically mean you have a good researcher. The difficult question is how reliably it makes progress over a long sequence of decisions, especially when there isn’t an easy signal telling it whether it’s right.

I’d expect automation to happen unevenly. Work with fast, clear feedback—some kinds of programming and experimentation, for example—is a more natural starting point. Humans may initially set the direction and evaluate results while agents do increasingly substantial pieces of the work. As systems become better at choosing experiments and checking their own conclusions, that division could shift.

And if they can contribute substantially to AI research itself, that creates the possibility of a feedback loop: better systems helping us build better systems. That’s a reason to pay attention to demonstrated research capability and the reliability of our oversight, rather than just whether something looks like an autonomous agent.
